titre: Salem: when the specter is no longer enough
accroche: Massachusetts, 1692: what stops the hangings at Salem is not doubt about witches, it is a question of proof.
contenu_vulgarise:
From February 1692 to May 1693, more than two hundred people are accused of witchcraft in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Thirty are found guilty, nineteen are hanged; one man, Giles Corey, dies under torture for refusing to enter a plea. Much of the case rests on what is called spectral evidence: young accusers claim to see the ghost, the apparition of a neighbor who has come to torment them. This testimony is almost impossible to refute, since no one else sees anything.

## Can the Devil take an innocent face?

The point debated by the ministers of the day is not whether witches exist. Everyone believes they do. It is narrower: for a neighbor's apparition to prove that the neighbor is a witch, the Devil must be able to borrow only the likeness of those who have given him their consent. Yet nothing establishes this.

As early as May 31, 1692, Cotton Mather writes to one of the judges, John Richards, not to give spectral evidence alone more weight than it can bear, since the Devil may have assumed the shape of blameless persons. After the first hanging, that of Bridget Bishop on June 10, the Boston ministers, consulted by Governor William Phips, deliver an opinion on June 15 that recommends caution. His father, Increase Mather, finishes on October 3, 1692 a book whose title says it all: *Cases of Conscience Concerning Evil Spirits Personating Men*.

He does not dispute the Devil or witchcraft. He even writes that facts attested by real witnesses, and not by specters, would suffice to root out the guilty. His argument is purely one of evidence: an apparition, which the Devil can fabricate at will, does not tell the guilty from the innocent; so it may raise suspicion but cannot support a conviction. He cites, in passing, a maxim he says is already old: better that a guilty person be acquitted than an innocent one condemned.

## A rule of evidence rather than a doubt

On October 12, 1692, Phips writes that he stopped the trials as soon as he understood the danger that the accusers' testimony alone posed to innocent subjects. The court is dissolved at the end of the month. A new court sits in January 1693, with firm limits on spectral evidence; almost all the accused are acquitted, and Phips pardons the last of those convicted.

In Mather's writings, the belief in witches remains intact. What changes is the quality demanded of testimony: one can keep one's certainties and still refuse to convict on a sign that the Devil himself could produce. It remains to ask how many of our own proofs would look like specters seen from so far away.

carte.punch: 1692: a neighbor's specter is no longer enough to hang him
carte.idee: At Salem, accusers claimed to see their neighbors' apparitions. Increase Mather, without doubting witchcraft, answers in 1692 that an apparition the Devil can fabricate is not enough to convict. He adds that it is better to see ten suspects acquitted than one innocent person condemned.

quiz.question: What argument does Increase Mather raise against spectral evidence in his Cases of Conscience?
choix: That the accusers were making up their visions, since witches do not exist
That only sworn adults could testify before a court
That English law forbade any conviction for witchcraft without a confession from the accused
That the Devil can take the appearance of an innocent person: the apparition proves nothing
quiz.explication: Mather denies neither the Devil nor witchcraft: he even admits that real witnesses would suffice to convict. His objection is about evidence: if the Devil can fabricate the apparition of an innocent person, it does not tell the guilty from the innocent and is not enough to convict. The other three answers attribute to him a skepticism, a rule of competence or an English law that he does not invoke.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many people are hanged at the end of the Salem trials, according to the entry?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of more than two hundred accused and thirty found guilty, nineteen are hanged; Giles Corey dies under torture for refusing to enter a plea.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Governor Phips say he stopped the trials, in his letter of October 12, 1692?
choix: Because the King of England orders him to directly
Because he himself doubts the existence of witchcraft
Because the accusers' testimony alone endangers innocent subjects
Because Cotton Mather threatens to resign as a minister
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Phips writes that he understood the danger that the accusers' testimony alone posed to innocent subjects, and dissolves the court at the end of October.
